title: Benchmarking Methodology
summary: Measuring performance rigorously enough to trust the number and act on it: controlling for warm-up and noise, reporting percentiles instead of averages, and the classic ways a benchmark quietly measures nothing.

slides.markdown:
[Profiling Techniques](profiling-techniques) finds *where* the time goes. Benchmarking answers the next question: did your fix actually help, and by how much? Get the methodology wrong and the answer is noise dressed up as a number.

A trustworthy benchmark controls for warm-up effects, reports a distribution rather than a single run, and measures a workload that resembles what production actually does. Skip any of those and you can "prove" a regression is a win, or watch the compiler quietly optimize your benchmark down to nothing.

This topic is the rigor layer underneath every optimization claim in this group — without it, "I made it faster" is an opinion, not a result.

slides.sectionTitle: What a benchmark must control for
slides.subTitle: Warm-up, noise, input realism
slides.markdown:
A benchmark number is only as trustworthy as the conditions that produced it. Three things have to be controlled, or the number reflects the environment rather than the code:

- **Warm-up.** Runtimes with a JIT (Java, .NET, Node's V8), CPU caches, and OS file caches all start cold and improve over the first several iterations. A benchmark that includes those cold iterations reports a blend of "cold performance" and "steady-state performance" that describes neither honestly.
- **Environment noise.** A shared CI runner, a laptop with Slack and a browser open, or a cloud VM on a noisy neighbor can all inject 10-30% variance unrelated to your code. Benchmarks need either a quiet, dedicated environment or enough repetitions to average the noise out statistically.
- **Input realism.** A benchmark fed unrealistic inputs (all-same-value, always-sorted, tiny) can make an algorithm look better or worse than it behaves on real data — this is the benchmarking-specific version of the "optimizing a benchmark that doesn't represent production" mistake from Performance Mindset & Measurement.

Control all three and the number means something; skip any one and you have a number, not a measurement.

slides.subTitle: What each can and can't tell you
slides.markdown:
A **microbenchmark** isolates one function or code path and runs it in a tight loop, millions of times, outside the rest of the system. It's precise and fast to run, and it's the right tool for comparing two implementations of the same narrow operation — e.g., which JSON parsing library is faster for a given payload shape.

A **system-level benchmark** (often called a load test or end-to-end benchmark) exercises the whole request path — network, application, database, caches — under conditions resembling real traffic. It's noisier and slower to run, but it's the only kind that reflects effects a microbenchmark can't see: contention, cache warmth across a real working set, connection pool exhaustion, GC pauses under sustained allocation.

The trap is drawing system-level conclusions from a microbenchmark: a microbenchmark showing algorithm A is 2x faster than B in isolation says nothing about whether that 2x survives once both run inside a system where A's memory access pattern happens to thrash a shared CPU cache under concurrent load. Use microbenchmarks to pick between clearly-defined narrow options; use system-level benchmarks to confirm the win survives contact with the rest of the system.

slides.subTitle: Why the first N iterations of a benchmark lie
slides.markdown:
Managed runtimes with a JIT compiler (the JVM, .NET's CLR, V8 for JavaScript) start by interpreting or running unoptimized machine code, then profile the running program and recompile hot functions into optimized native code — but only after they've run enough times to be identified as hot. That takes anywhere from dozens to thousands of invocations depending on the runtime.

A benchmark that measures from the very first call captures mostly interpreter or baseline-JIT performance, which can be 5-10x slower than the steady-state optimized code the function will actually run at in a long-lived production process. Reporting that number as "the" performance of the function is measuring the wrong regime entirely.

The fix is a deliberate **warm-up phase**: run the benchmarked code enough times to reach steady state (JIT tools like JMH make this explicit with separate "warm-up iterations" and "measurement iterations"), discard the warm-up results, and only report timing from iterations after the runtime has stopped improving. Skipping warm-up is the single most common reason two people benchmarking the "same" code on the same machine get wildly different numbers.

slides.subTitle: Report a distribution, not a single number
slides.markdown:
A single run's average hides exactly the information that matters. Run the same benchmark 100 times and you'll get a distribution, not a constant — and that distribution's shape is the actual result.

What to report instead of one number:

- **Multiple runs, not one.** A single run can land anywhere in the noise; run enough repetitions to see the spread.
- **Percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not just the mean.** A mean can look great while p99 is terrible — exactly the average-vs-tail trap covered in Latency Optimization. Two benchmarks with identical means can represent very different real experiences if one has a long tail and the other doesn't.
- **Variance or confidence interval.** "14ms ± 0.3ms" is a claim you can act on. "14ms" alone might be one lucky run out of a distribution centered at 20ms.

A benchmark result reported as a bare single number — "the new version is 12ms" — should be treated as unverified until you know how many runs produced it and what the spread looked like. This is exactly the discipline a scientific experiment requires, and performance claims deserve the same standard.

slides.subTitle: Measuring nothing and not noticing

slides.markdown:
| | Benchmarking in isolation | Benchmarking under concurrent load |
|---|---|---|
| **What it measures** | Single-threaded, uncontended cost of an operation | Behavior when many callers compete for the same resources |
| **Catches** | Algorithmic cost, per-call overhead | Lock contention, connection-pool exhaustion, false sharing, cache-line contention |
| **Misses** | Everything contention-related | Nothing structural, but individual numbers are noisier |
| **Example finding** | "This function takes 2μs" | "This function takes 2μs alone, but 40μs when 50 threads call it concurrently because they all block on the same mutex" |

A function can look completely fine in isolation and fall apart under concurrent load, because isolation benchmarks structurally cannot see lock contention — there's no second thread to contend with. This is why Concurrency Performance work always needs a concurrent-load benchmark, not a single-threaded one, to validate: an isolated microbenchmark answering "is this fast" is a different, narrower question than "does this scale."

slides.subTitle: Catching slow creep before it ships
slides.markdown:
The benchmarks discussed so far are one-off: run once, compare two variants, decide. **Regression benchmarking** runs the same benchmark on every commit (or nightly) and tracks the metric over time, specifically to catch a *slow creep* — no single commit regresses performance by an alarming amount, but ten commits each adding 2% eventually add up to a 20% regression that nobody noticed because no one commit crossed a threshold.

Making this work in practice requires the same rigor as any other benchmark, applied continuously: a dedicated, low-noise runner (shared CI hardware with variable load defeats the purpose), enough repetitions per run to get a stable number, and an alert threshold tuned to the environment's actual noise floor — too tight and it cries wolf on every run, too loose and it never fires.

Teams that run this well treat a benchmark regression the same as a failing test: it blocks the PR (or at minimum requires an explicit acknowledgment) rather than becoming a graph nobody looks at until someone notices the service got slow three months later.

Proving a fix helped requires a controlled comparison, not two numbers from two different circumstances. The most common way this goes wrong: benchmarking the "before" version on a busy laptop last Tuesday and the "after" version on a quiet CI runner today, then attributing the entire difference to the code change.

A valid before/after comparison holds everything else constant: same machine (or same class of machine, ideally the same physical one), same input data, same warm-up protocol, same time of day if the environment has diurnal load patterns, and — critically — both variants run in the *same* session, ideally interleaved (run A, run B, run A, run B...) rather than sequentially, so a machine-wide slowdown partway through affects both equally rather than only one.

When the difference is small relative to the noise floor you measured in §2 and §5, a simple significance check (or at minimum, confirming the confidence intervals don't overlap) is what separates "we measured an improvement" from "we measured noise and a placebo." A 3% win reported without knowing the run-to-run variance is not a result.

Before writing the benchmark, decide what question it's answering — this determines everything about how it's built. "Is implementation A faster than B for this exact operation" wants a controlled microbenchmark. "Will this change survive production traffic" wants a system-level or shadow-traffic test. "Did we regress over the last month" wants a tracked CI benchmark.

A common failure is building a microbenchmark to answer a system-level question — proving a cache implementation is fast in isolation, then shipping it and discovering it thrashes under real concurrent access patterns the microbenchmark never modeled. The benchmark wasn't wrong; it was answering a narrower question than the one being asked of it.

Stating the question up front also tells you what "done" looks like: a microbenchmark is done when the numbers are stable and reproducible; a regression benchmark is never "done," it runs forever as a tripwire. Knowing which one you're building prevents both under-investing in rigor (treating a one-off comparison casually) and over-investing (building CI infrastructure for a question you only needed to answer once).

slides.sectionTitle: A trustworthy benchmark, end to end
slides.markdown:
Putting the pieces together, a benchmark you can act on: states the question it's answering (§10), picks the right shape for that question — microbenchmark, system-level, or continuous regression tracking (§3, §8) — runs a proper warm-up before measuring (§4), uses realistic inputs and controls environment noise (§2), reports a distribution and percentiles rather than one number (§5), defeats dead-code elimination (§6), and — if concurrency matters at all — tests under realistic concurrent load, not just in isolation (§7).

Skip any step and the number you get back is still a number — it just isn't evidence. The next two topics, Algorithmic & Data Structure Optimization and Latency Optimization, are where you spend the wins a rigorous benchmark actually confirms; without this methodology underneath them, you can't tell a real win from a lucky run.
